opus-5.5.text:
Well, thanks for having me. I think what draws me to robots as an artistic medium is that they sit right at this fascinating boundary between the natural and the artificial. A robot is a machine, but it moves through physical space, it interacts with real objects, and when it does that, people instinctively start projecting intentions and personality onto it. That tension is really rich territory for an artist.

And there's something else I find compelling. Robots are surprisingly clumsy. We have this cultural image, largely from science fiction, of robots as precise, all-powerful, maybe even threatening. But anyone who works with them in a lab knows they're constantly fumbling, dropping things, misreading the world. I find that gap between the myth and the reality really interesting, and art is a wonderful way to explore it. It lets you ask questions that a technical paper can't, like: what does it mean for a machine to be uncertain? What does it mean for us to trust something we can only see through a camera or control from a distance?

Some of my earliest projects, like the Telegarden back in the mid-nineties, were really about that. We put a robot arm in a garden and let people all over the world tend it over the internet. On the surface it was about gardening, but underneath it was about questions of presence and authenticity. How do you know the garden is real? How do you know your actions actually mattered? Those are epistemological questions, and I think robots, because they bridge the digital and the physical, are a unique way to raise them.

So for me the art and the research feed each other. The art lets me step back and reflect on what we're actually building and why, and that often comes back around and changes how I think about the engineering.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts science fiction’s image of robots as precise and all-powerful with their real-world clumsiness, and says art can explore that gap.

r002.rationale: It describes robots’ cultural image from science fiction and people’s tendency to project intentions and personality onto them as part of their artistic appeal.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it goes back to the fact that robots sit right at this boundary between the physical and the virtual, between what we imagine machines can do and what they actually can do. And that gap is where a lot of interesting things happen, not just for engineering but for art.

When I started doing art with robots back in the nineties, part of what drew me in was that people have these very strong preconceptions. They've seen Terminator, they've seen the Jetsons, and they bring all of that to the encounter. So a robot is already a loaded object before it does anything. As an artist, that's a gift, because you can play with those expectations, confirm them, subvert them, make people uncomfortable or make them laugh.

The other thing is that robots force you to confront questions about agency and authenticity. One of the early projects I did was the Telegarden, where people on the internet could control a robot arm to plant and water seeds in a real garden. And the question people kept asking was, is this real? Am I actually doing this, or is it a simulation? That tension, which I've called telepistemology, the question of what we can know at a distance through a technological medium, turned out to be a deep philosophical issue. And it's only gotten more relevant as more of our lives are mediated by screens and networks.

And then frankly, there's the fact that robots are imperfect. They're clumsy, they fail, they do unexpected things. In my engineering work I'm trying to eliminate that uncertainty. But in art, the uncertainty is the interesting part. It's a reminder that these machines aren't the omniscient, all-capable things we tend to fantasize about. There's a humility in that, and I think art is a good way to communicate it to people who aren't going to read the research papers.

r001.rationale: The response describes using robots in art to play with, subvert, and challenge people's expectations of what machines can do.

r002.rationale: It says robots carry strong preconceptions from cultural images such as the Terminator and the Jetsons, making them a culturally loaded artistic medium.

astra-6.text:
For me, robots bring together two things I love: the precision of engineering and the ambiguity of art. When you’re building a robot as an engineer, you’re trying to make its behavior reliable and predictable. But as an artist, you can use that same machine to raise questions, to create something that doesn’t have a single correct interpretation.

And there’s something compelling about a machine moving in physical space. We tend to attribute intention to it. Even a very simple movement can seem hesitant, curious, or stubborn. That gap between what the machine is actually doing and what we imagine it’s doing is a rich place to work as an artist.

r001.rationale: It contrasts engineering reliability with art’s ambiguity, but does not identify challenging conventional wisdom about technology as a purpose of robot art.

r002.rationale: It mentions that viewers attribute intention to a robot’s movements, but does not explain the medium’s interest through accumulated cultural associations.

sol-6.1.text:
What interests me is that robots bring ideas into contact with the physical world. You can have a beautiful, precise description of what a machine should do, but then it encounters friction, uncertainty, something you didn’t anticipate. That gap between the ideal and the real is fascinating to me, both as an engineer and as an artist.

And robots invite us to think about ourselves. We see a machine move and almost immediately start attributing intention to it. Does it know what it’s doing? Is it hesitating? As an artistic medium, that gives you a way to explore perception, control, and our relationship with technology. The robot doesn’t necessarily have to be impressive technically; sometimes a very simple action can raise an interesting question.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the gap between a machine’s intended behavior and reality, and how people perceive robots, but does not identify challenging conventional wisdom about technology as a purpose of using robots in art.

r002.rationale: It describes people attributing intention to robots and exploring our relationship with technology, but does not explain the medium’s appeal in terms of robots’ accumulated cultural associations.
